paragraphs: Swamiji once asked the saint Pavhari Baba why he stayed inside his cave instead of coming out to help the world. The Baba, humble and full of humour as always, first answered with a story that packed quite a punch.

There was once a crook who was caught in a crime, and as punishment his nose was cut off. Too ashamed to show his face and sick of himself, he ran away into a forest. There he laid out a tiger-skin, and whenever he sensed someone nearby he would put on a show of deep meditation.

Instead of keeping people away, this drew them in. Crowds came to bow before the wonderful forest saint, and soon he was living comfortably once again. Years went by, and the villagers grew eager to hear some teaching from the silent holy man. One young man in particular kept begging to be initiated as his disciple, and the pressure grew so great that further delay would have damaged the saint's reputation.

So at last the saint spoke. He told the young man to come back the next day with a sharp razor. Overjoyed, the youth showed up early. The saint led him to a lonely corner of the forest, took the razor and, in one stroke, sliced off the young man's nose. Then he solemnly announced that this had been his own initiation, and that the disciple must faithfully pass it on to others when the chance came.

The young man was too embarrassed to reveal what had really happened, so he obeyed. And that, said the Baba with a twinkle, is how a whole sect of noseless saints spread across the land. Did Swamiji want him to start another one?
Later, when asked more seriously, the Baba gave a different answer. Is physical help the only kind there is? Might one mind not help other minds without the body doing anything at all?
learn: Wearing the look of wisdom without the substance can fool people for a while, and pretence tends to spread. It also shows that quiet inner work, done sincerely, can be a real form of service, even when it isn't visible.
